reference: Runnable cases use Bash's documented type/help metadata contract and fixed help phrases documented by the sysctl builtin in loadables/sysctl.c. No operation oracle was run: GNU procps-ng behavior must be compared later in a disposable VM with a private /proc/sys fixture or reviewed syscall mock.
coverage: Bash metadata: builtin classification, type description, and documented help synopsis/options.
Deferred: named key reads and filters; recursive dump; argument writes; configuration loading and precedence.
exclusions: No sysctl operation is executed under this safety scope, including read-only access to /proc/sys.
No parity claim is made; the system Bash reference has no sysctl builtin and using GNU sysctl would access system kernel parameters.

cases.purpose: Bash type metadata identifies the registered sysctl command as a builtin.
The Bash type builtin reports the command as a shell builtin, not an external executable.
Bash help exposes the documented query syntax and representative value/name/pattern options without invoking a sysctl operation.
cases.script:
doc=$(help sysctl)
[[ $doc == *"Read and write kernel parameters via /proc/sys."* ]] || exit 1
[[ $doc == *"sysctl KEY [KEY ...]"* ]] || exit 1
[[ $doc == *"-n/--values value-only, -N/--names names-only,"* ]] || exit 1
[[ $doc == *"-r/--pattern EXPR filter keys by regex"* ]] || exit 1
printf 'sysctl help contract ok\n'

cases.purpose: Compare dotted-key reads, -n/-N output, -e unknown-key handling, and -r filtering with deterministic values.
cases.reason: Not a capability block: procps-ng 4.0.4 /usr/sbin/sysctl is in the guest image and on the legacy reference PATH, so a byte oracle exists. Read-only /proc/sys access is unprivileged; the legacy bwrap procfs exposes it. Many keys are per-namespace and deterministic in a fresh namespace, identical for both sides: kernel.hostname (bwrap sets 'parity'), kernel.domainname, net.ipv4.ip_default_ttl / net.ipv4.ip_forward in the fresh netns, fs.mqueue.msg_max and kernel.shmmni in the fresh IPC ns, kernel.ostype, kernel.osrelease. A USERNS in the plain driver owns its UTS/net/IPC namespaces, so writes to those namespaced keys are permitted and confined to it. A per-side bind mount of a fixture tree over /proc/sys, or of fixture dirs over /etc/sysctl.d and siblings, in the child's mount namespace (preflight) gives a fixed tree for both candidate and procps, which both hardcode /proc/sys. No fixture exists.

cases.purpose: Compare -a/-A recursive key enumeration, readable values, and treatment of unreadable entries against a small fixed tree.
cases.reason: No privilege is needed, but a fixed tree requires each side to bind-mount a fixture directory over /proc/sys in its own mount namespace. Mounting needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN over that namespace: a USERNS has it, while the legacy runner disables user namespaces and plain uid 2000 gets EPERM. No fixture exists. Alternatively, restrict live dumps to a namespaced deterministic subtree with -r.

cases.purpose: Compare -w and implicit KEY=VALUE writes, echo and -q behavior, unknown keys, and documented read-only key errors while inspecting resulting fixture values.
cases.reason: Not a capability block. Writes to namespaced keys (kernel.hostname/domainname in an owned UTS ns, net.ipv4.* in an owned netns, fs.mqueue.* in an owned IPC ns) are allowed for root in a USERNS and die with it. Permission errors are reachable as plain uid 2000. No fixture exists.

cases.purpose: Compare -p parsing of relative fixture files and --system file ordering/precedence using deterministic configuration inputs.
cases.reason: No privilege is needed. In a USERNS, -p with namespaced keys and fixture dirs bind-mounted over the absolute config locations are confined to the child. No fixture exists.
